title: A shabad for your home
hook: many families have a shabad they keep for their house

segments.voice: Yesterday, sooraa, and your line: accepted in his court. Did you live one brave, true hour? We've sung through weddings and funerals. Today the shabads come home, to an ordinary house on an ordinary day. Day six hundred seventy-six.

In some Sikh homes, the shabad is on the wall before anyone sings it: a framed line of Gurmukhi by the front door, or above the stove, or in the hallway. Ask about it, and you'll often get a story. It was my grandmother's favorite. My dad sang it when we moved from Kenya. We played it the night the baby came home. Families have songs the way they have recipes, passed down without anyone deciding to. In some Sikh households, one of those songs is a shabad. Today: a shabad for your home.
screen: `A FRAMED LINE BY THE DOOR.` → `EVERY LINE HAS A STORY.` → `SONGS PASSED DOWN LIKE RECIPES.`

segments.voice: Shabad means word, and in Sikh life it means a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word sung. There's no rule that a family must have one shabad of its own. But some do, and it happens in ordinary ways. A house is blessed with a reading of Sukhmani Sahib and an Ardas when a family moves in, and one line from that day sticks. A grandmother hums the same hymn every evening for years, and her grandchildren hum it without knowing the words. A parent sings one to a child at bedtime, and it becomes theirs. Some keep a well-loved line, like dukh bhanjan teraa naam. In paraphrase, it says: Your Name destroys pain. That shabad of Guru Arjan, on Ang two eighteen, goes on: dwell on it through all the hours of the day; this is the perfect True Guru's wisdom. Others choose taatee vaao na lagaee, the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Anand Sahib's opening joy. Why does it matter? Because a household shabad works like a family's memory. It's there at the birthday and at the hospital, sung in the car and over the dishes. When something hard happens, nobody has to search for words. The words are already in the house, worn smooth by use. And there's a deeper Sikh idea underneath: the Guru isn't kept only in the gurdwara. The Word can live where you live, in the kitchen and the hallway, sung by people in their socks.
screen: `SHABAD: THE WORD, SUNG.` · `HOW A FAMILY GETS ITS HYMN.` · `DUKH BHANJAN: YOUR NAME ENDS PAIN.` · `THE WORD LIVES WHERE YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `OUR SHABAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a shabad for your home. Sit, and think back over the lines you've met on this path. Which one would you want in your house: by the door, at bedtime, on a hard day? Maybe a line from the laavan, maybe the hot wind, maybe the Name that ends pain. Let one rise. Say its words, or its meaning, silently, as if you were saying it in your own kitchen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after it. The bell holds the time.

Dukh bhanjan, destroyer of pain: one well-loved line families keep, like dukh bhanjan teraa naam, sung at birthdays and hospital beds, passed down like a recipe, so the words are already there when they're needed.
Your line: our shabad. Today, write the line you chose somewhere in your home where you'll see it, or share it with someone you live with. Day six hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some Sikh families keep a favorite shabad for their home: framed by the door, sung at bedtime or on family occasions, often first heard at a house blessing with Sukhmani Sahib and Ardas.
